item.title: 【AI4S】 Filter By:
item.description: Artificial intelligence for combinatorial optimization depends on high-quality, structured training data, yet transforming ambiguous natural-language descriptions into precise, executable formal models remains a major bottleneck, traditionally requiring extensive manual effort and domain expertise. We develop CPAM-LLM, an automated constraint-programming modeling framework based on large language models that converts unstructured problem specifications into validated and executable formal models. The framework integrates retrieval-augmented generation grounded in formal concept analysis for structural validation, chaos-mapping-based data augmentation to enhance cross-domain generalization, and dynamic constraint adaptation to accommodate evolving problem settings. We demonstrate its effectiveness across five scenarios, including DNA sequence design, reconfigurable energy storage systems, and unmanned vehicle logistics. item.title: 【Self-driving laboratories】 Filter By:
item.description: Autonomous scientists enabled by large language models and agentic reasoning have become a compelling narrative for accelerating research. Here we pose that labaoratory autonomy is not primarily a text problem, as experiments have to be run in the world of instrument-addressable actions and constraints, and planned based on costs, latencies and rewards. We argue for a bottom-up foundation for self-driving laboratories that complements language-first planning by introducing frameworks that translate hypotheses into decisions executable on real tools. We propose three operational principles. First, self-driving laboratories should adopt an information-efficiency objective that maximizes decision-relevant information per unit experimental cost. This requires combining comprehensive data acquisition with minimal, decisive experimental design. Second, hypotheses should be compiled into experimental footprints defined by accessible actions, constraints, observables and decision rules.
